drop/layer: Here is a hidden layer's output, h: four units, with values two, one, three and two.
drop/mask: During training, dropout keeps each unit with probability p, here a half, and zeroes the rest. A random mask, m, decides: a one keeps a unit, and a zero drops it. This time it keeps units zero and two.
drop/kept: On average, a fraction p of the units stay: four units times a half, two. Each step draws a new mask, so which two changes.
drop/zeroed: Multiply h by m, entry by entry, and the layer's output becomes two, zero, three, zero.
drop/scale: Then the kept units are divided by p. With p a half, that doubles them: four, zero, six, zero. This is inverted dropout.
drop/why: Why divide? A unit is kept only a fraction p of the time. Dividing by p makes up for it: on average, p times h over p is h, exactly what the unit gives without dropout.
drop/plain: Plain dropout skips the division, so a kept unit passes h as it is. Then unit zero averages a half times two, plus a half times zero: one. That is p times h, smaller than h.
test/test: At test time, every unit is kept and nothing is scaled. The layer passes h straight through: two, one, three, two.
test/match: Because training already divided by p, the next layer sees at test time what it saw on average in training. No correction is needed.
test/plain: Plain dropout never divided, so at test time it keeps every unit and multiplies each output by p instead: two, one, three, two become one, a half, one and a half, one. That matches its training average, p times h.
test/lean: And in training, any unit might vanish at any moment, so no unit can count on another being there. Each has to be useful on its own.
